html:
Satuq Bughra Khan, a ruler of the Kara-Khanid Turks at Kashgar, became a Muslim in the first half of the 10th century. The traditional date is around 934. He is remembered as the first Turkic khan to convert to Islam.

The story comes mostly from later Muslim tradition and is partly legend. It says that he learned about Islam from Muslim merchants and scholars coming from the Samanid lands to the west, and that he had to fight his uncle, the ruling khan, to take power. He died around 955 and is buried at Artux near Kashgar, where his tomb is still visited.

Why it matters:

  • The Kara-Khanids became the first Turkic dynasty to make Islam the state religion.
  • In 999 they took Bukhara from the Samanids and ruled Transoxiana, a Turkic Muslim state in an old Persian heartland.
  • From Kashgar, Islam spread east into the Tarim Basin, which had long been Buddhist. The Buddhist kingdom of Khotan fell to Kara-Khanid armies in the early 11th century.

This conversion was an early step in a larger change. Over the next centuries most Turkic peoples of the Turkic migrations became Muslim, and Turkic soldiers and rulers came to dominate much of the Islamic world. A century later, the Kara-Khanid scholar Mahmud al-Kashgari wrote his great dictionary of Turkic for Arabic-speaking readers.
sum: Satuq Bughra Khan, a ruler of the Kara-Khanid Turks at Kashgar, became a Muslim in the first half of the 10th century. The traditional date is around 934. He is remembered as the first Turkic khan to convert to Islam.
